extracted.intended_audience: law students, lawyers, judges, policymakers, and general readers interested in U.S. administrative law and judicial review of agency rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the Supreme Court's articulation of the 'arbitrary-or-capricious' standard (including hard-look review) for judicial review of agency rulemakings and the statutory expectations for agency decisionmaking under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act and the APA. Useful for understanding what courts require agencies to explain and consider when promulgating, changing, or rescinding regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary-or-capricious test
rubrics_metrics.description: A legal standard of review (from the Administrative Procedure Act) instructing courts to invalidate agency actions that are 'arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law.' Most frequently employed to assess the factual basis of an agency's rulemaking, especially informal rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by reviewing courts to determine whether an agency's rule should be set aside. The page explains the test's role and situates it as the principal standard for judicial review of agency action under the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must examine relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must 'examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for its action, including a 'rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance from the Court: reviewing courts should consider whether the decision was based on a consideration of relevant factors and whether there has been a clear error of judgment. Courts will not substitute their judgment for the agency's, but the agency must supply the reasoned basis; courts may 'uphold a decision of less than ideal clarity if the agency's path may reasonably be discerned.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated defects that make a rule arbitrary or capricious
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency rule is normally arbitrary and capricious if the agency has (1) relied on factors Congress did not intend it to consider, (2) entirely failed to consider an important aspect of the problem, (3) offered an explanation that runs counter to the evidence before the agency, or (4) made a decision so implausible that it could not be ascribed to a difference in view or agency expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list (from the Court's opinion) functions as a checklist of common flaws courts identify when invalidating agency actions. Examples on the page apply these failings to NHTSA's revocation of the passive-restraint requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard look review (endorsed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard look review requires that courts ensure agencies take account of all relevant facts, make reasonable policy choices, explain their behavior in detail, and consider policy alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State Farm endorsed hard look review as an application of the arbitrary-or-capricious test. The page notes the practical effect: courts can require reasoned analysis and consideration of alternatives from agencies before upholding rulemaking changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory substantive standard for vehicle safety rules (NTMVSA): reasonable, practicable, and appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act, the agency must issue vehicle safety standards 'based on relevant motor vehicle safety data' and that are 'reasonable, practicable and appropriate to further vehicle safety.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the case, NHTSA invoked the statute's reasonableness/practicability requirement in deciding to rescind the passive-restraint rule; the page uses this statute to explain how statutory commands interact with arbitrary-or-capricious review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record compilation and substantial-evidence support on review
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress required a record of the rulemaking proceedings to be compiled and submitted to a reviewing court, and intended that agency findings under the Act be supported by 'substantial evidence on the record considered as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence of a compiled rulemaking record and substantial-evidence support is relevant when courts review agency findings; lack of an adequate record or insufficient evidentiary support can render an action arbitrary or capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to consider alternatives and specific regulatory options
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must consider relevant alternatives and specific options that bear on the issue (e.g., here, whether requiring non-detachable passive seatbelts or whether installing airbags would satisfy the safety standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The DC Circuit faulted NHTSA for not adequately considering non-detachable seatbelts or whether airbags alone would satisfy the standard; State Farm reiterates that failure to consider important aspects or alternatives can be arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of review: narrow but meaningful (courts should not substitute their judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of review under the arbitrary-or-capricious standard is narrow; a court should not substitute its judgment for that of the agency, yet the agency must provide a rational basis for its choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This balances judicial restraint with the requirement that agencies explain their choices. The Court instructs judges to uphold rules if the agency's path may reasonably be discerned, but not to invent a reasoned basis the agency did not provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change in administration can justify re-evaluation if within statutory bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A change in administration may be a reasonable basis for an agency to re-evaluate costs and benefits of a program or regulation, provided the re-evaluation and resulting decision remain within the bounds set by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Rehnquist (concurring in part, dissenting in part) argued that the agency's change of position appeared related to a new administration and that such a change can justify re-assessment; however, the agency must still meet the arbitrary-or-capricious standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency interpretations may be reinforced by congressional inaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency interpretations of statutes can 'be confirmed or ratified by subsequent congressional failure to change that interpretation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State Farm notes that while congressional inaction may be evidence supporting an agency interpretation, such interpretations remain subject to the arbitrary-or-capricious test and must still be reasonably explained.
